prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: whether the home policy covers flooding. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 4)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the claim follows heavy rain or a swollen river, I still check the policy wording for the exact flood definition; surface water, groundwater and overflowing watercourses can be treated differently, so I should not assume one trigger covers all."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the customer has buildings cover, flood damage to the structure is usually considered under that section first, but I still need to confirm any exclusions, endorsements and the excess before I treat it as covered."},{"type":"observation","content":"When water enters through a damaged roof, blocked gutter or failed seal during a storm, I should separate storm-related ingress from flood, because not every water-damage claim after bad weather is flood cover."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the policy specifically excludes gradual seepage, wear and tear, or lack of maintenance, I should not label the loss as flood just because there was water inside; the source and cause must match the cover."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a nearby drain backs up and water rises from below ground level, I should check whether the wording treats that as flood, escape of water or sewer backing up, since the cover pathway can change the outcome."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the claim is borderline, I prefer to ask for a simple timeline of how the water got in before I decide on cover, because the sequence of events is often more important than the amount of water."},{"type":"fact","content":"When contents are damaged by flood, I need to check that the policy includes contents cover at the address and that any high-risk-item limits, item limits or single-item limits do not affect the assessment."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the customer mentions an ongoing flood alert or repeated inundation, I should look for any policy condition about reasonable precautions, as failing to move valuables or shut off vulnerable areas may affect the claim handling even where flood is insured."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the property is unoccupied for a long period, flood cover may still exist but be subject to special terms, so I must check the unoccupied-property conditions before accepting cover at face value."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the evidence is unclear, I should use the Met Office information, local weather reports and the claim photos together to decide whether the event was a flood event under the wording, rather than relying on the customer’s label alone."}]}
